prompt_free_text:
This paper studies a simple but important mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful proof trajectories, yet at inference time they operate inside a search process that repeatedly proposes tactics, observes failures, and backtracks. The paper proposes to train on trial-and-error traces that include failed branches and backtracking decisions, and evaluates this idea on a newly constructed Lean dataset for intuitionistic propositional logic, PropL. The central empirical claim is that a model trained with such traces, TrialMaster, achieves higher success rates and lower search cost than a conventional tactic generator trained only on successful proofs.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially valuable. The core intuition is sound, the setting is clean enough to isolate the effect of failure-aware training, and the dataset contribution could be useful for future controlled studies of theorem proving with LLMs. At the same time, the current version has several methodological and presentation issues that make it difficult to fully assess the strength and generality of the conclusions. My assessment is therefore positive but cautious.

The main strength of the paper is that it identifies a real train-test discrepancy in theorem proving systems and addresses it in a direct way. Much prior work indeed trains on gold proof steps while relying on search-time exploration to recover from mistakes. The idea of exposing the model to failed attempts and backtracking histories is natural, and the paper provides a concrete implementation rather than only a conceptual argument. I also appreciate that the authors choose a formalized domain in Lean, where correctness can be checked exactly, and that they attempt to construct a representative theorem distribution rather than relying on a narrow hand-curated benchmark.

The dataset contribution is also meaningful. A benchmark with complete proof-search traces, including failed branches, is genuinely useful because such data are scarce in public theorem-proving corpora. The use of a theorem generator based on a bijection between natural numbers and formulas is an appealing way to avoid obvious sampling biases over syntax, and the use of a deterministic proof-search procedure gives a principled source of supervision. If released cleanly, this dataset could support follow-up work on imitation learning from search, offline RL for proving, or calibration of tactic models under backtracking.

That said, the paper’s empirical story is less clean than it first appears, because the comparisons are not always apples-to-apples. The headline comparison is between TrialMaster, which emits one tactic or a backtrack instruction greedily while conditioning on the full search history, and a DFS baseline that samples multiple tactics per state with tuned temperature and branching factor. These are substantially different inference paradigms. TrialMaster is not merely “the same model trained with failure data”; it is also given a richer action space and a different control loop. The paper partly addresses this with an ablation where a model trained without trial-and-error data is evaluated under the same one-step inference protocol, and this is in fact the most convincing result in the paper. However, the presentation overemphasizes the comparison to DFS and underemphasizes the cleaner ablation. The paper would be much stronger if the primary claim were framed around matched-inference comparisons, with DFS treated as a secondary systems baseline.

Relatedly, the reported numbers are somewhat confusing and raise concerns about consistency. Table 3 appears twice with conflicting values for TrialMaster on the OOD task, once as 69.3% and once as 88.7%. This is a serious presentation issue because it directly affects the main conclusion. The text also states that the difference between TrialMaster and the ablated model is 10.0%, which matches 69.3 versus 59.3, but not 88.7 versus 59.3. Such inconsistencies make it hard to trust the exact empirical claims. The paper needs careful proofreading and correction of all tables, captions, and references before it can be properly evaluated.

A second major concern is the extent to which the results reflect learning to reason from failure versus learning the idiosyncrasies of a specific proof-search algorithm and serialization format. The trial-and-error traces are generated by FPS with randomized choices during chaining, and the model is trained to imitate these traces, including explicit backtrack instructions. This may teach the model to emulate the search policy used to generate the data rather than to internalize a more general notion of “failed tactics should be downweighted.” In a narrow benchmark this may be acceptable, but the paper currently overstates the conceptual generality of the result. To support the broader claim, I would like to see stronger evidence that the benefit is not merely due to policy imitation. For example, one could compare against a model trained on successful proofs augmented with explicit state identifiers and prior attempted tactics, but without failed branches; or train on traces from one search policy and test under another; or evaluate whether the model avoids repeating previously failed tactics even when the exact trace format differs from training.

The dataset construction also deserves more scrutiny. The authors claim PropL is “complete, scalable, and representative,” but these terms are used somewhat loosely. The theorem generator may be representative over formulas under the chosen syntactic enumeration, but the actual training set is filtered by proof-length quantiles and restricted to formulas with exactly 16 internal nodes. This means the final benchmark distribution is not simply uniform over formulas, and the train/test split is intentionally stratified by proof difficulty. That is a reasonable design choice, but it weakens the claim of representativeness. Moreover, the proof-search procedure is made intentionally incomplete by forbidding an implication from being used to show its own premise, and while the authors say this affects only about 1 in 1000 provable theorems, this still means the proof corpus is not fully faithful to the underlying logic. The paper should be more precise and modest in describing these properties.

I also have concerns about the fairness of the stopping criteria. TrialMaster fails immediately upon any Lean error, whereas the DFS baseline can continue exploring alternative tactics after invalid suggestions at a state, since it samples multiple candidates and backtracks structurally. This asymmetry could either help or hurt TrialMaster depending on error frequency, but in any case it complicates interpretation. Similarly, the 1500-word context limit is stricter for TrialMaster because its prompt includes failed branches and backtracking history. The paper acknowledges this, but then uses success rate and Lean-call count as if they were directly comparable. A more informative evaluation would report failure breakdowns: percentage failing due to context overflow, invalid tactic syntax, semantic Lean errors, exhausted search budget, or repeated loops. That would clarify where the gains actually come from.

The search-cost metric, total number of Lean calls, is sensible for this setting, but it is not sufficient on its own. TrialMaster may use fewer Lean calls because backtrack instructions are “free,” but generating and processing long prompts with full proof histories also incurs substantial model-side cost. Since the paper’s framing emphasizes efficiency, it would be useful to report wall-clock time, average number of model decoding steps, average prompt length over the search, and perhaps total tokens processed. Otherwise, the efficiency claim is only partial: it measures proof-assistant calls but not total computational cost.

The experimental setup is otherwise somewhat underdeveloped for a conference paper. Training is done for a single epoch on two A100s, but there is little detail on prompt formatting, maximum sequence length, optimizer settings beyond learning rate, whether LoRA or full fine-tuning is used, how many total training examples result from selecting two proofs per theorem, or whether results are averaged across random seeds. Given the stochasticity in proof selection and model fine-tuning, seed variance is important. The paper reports point estimates on 1000 OOD theorems, but no confidence intervals or significance tests. Since some claimed differences are small, especially against tuned DFS baselines, uncertainty estimates are necessary.

The exploratory study on proof length is interesting but currently too speculative. The result that shorter trial-and-error traces outperform randomly selected longer ones could mean many things: reduced noise, easier optimization, less context truncation, or a mismatch between training and inference distributions. The explanation that “too many failed search paths may lower the quality of the training data” is plausible but not demonstrated. This section would benefit from more controlled analysis, such as fixing theorem subsets and varying only trace length, or measuring how often long-trace-trained models fail due to verbosity versus tactic quality.

Another limitation is external validity. The domain is intuitionistic propositional logic, where the tactic space is small, proof states are relatively regular, and proof search can be generated algorithmically at scale. This is an excellent testbed for controlled experimentation, but it is far from modern interactive theorem proving over rich mathematical libraries. The paper acknowledges this, but some claims in the introduction and conclusion still read too broadly. I would encourage the authors to position the work more explicitly as a proof-of-concept in a synthetic-but-formal domain, rather than evidence that failure-aware fine-tuning broadly improves theorem proving with LLMs.

There are also several writing and organization issues. The paper contains duplicated table numbering, inconsistent references to figures and tables, grammatical errors, and some awkward phrasing. The methodology section could be clearer about exactly what the model input and output look like. For example, when TrialMaster “outputs the entire proof path after,” but only the first tactic is used, it is unclear why generating the whole continuation is preferable to next-action prediction. Likewise, the serialization of states, tactics, and backtrack instructions should be shown concretely. Since the contribution hinges on the representation of trial-and-error history, this level of detail matters.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has a solid core. The matched ablation comparing a model trained with trial-and-error traces to one trained without them, under the same inference protocol, is the key result and appears promising. If the reported gain is correct and reproducible, that is meaningful evidence that failure-aware supervision helps in this domain. The dataset itself is also likely to be useful. My main reservation is that the paper currently mixes this clean message with broader claims and less controlled comparisons.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following. First, fix all inconsistencies in the reported results and provide complete tables for all main experiments, including exact TrialMaster success rate, Lean-call count, and failure-mode breakdown. Second, elevate the matched ablation to the primary experiment and clearly separate “effect of training data” from “effect of inference algorithm.” Third, add variance estimates across multiple fine-tuning runs and, if possible, across different random selections of trial-and-error traces. Fourth, provide more detail on prompt format and model training. Fifth, include analyses that probe whether the model truly uses failure information, such as measuring repetition of previously failed tactics, ablations on removing failed branches from the prompt at test time, or perturbing backtrack histories. Sixth, moderate the claims about representativeness and generality.

In summary, this is a worthwhile paper with a good idea, a potentially useful dataset, and encouraging empirical evidence, but the current version falls short of the rigor expected for a top-tier ML venue due to inconsistencies in results, imperfectly controlled comparisons, and limited analysis of mechanism and generality. I would lean borderline positive if the numerical issues are minor and the dataset/code are solid, but in its present form I would want a stronger revision before full endorsement.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset for intuitionistic propositional logic theorem proving that includes trial-and-error proof traces generated by a focused proof search procedure. Using this dataset, the authors fine-tune an LLM (Llama-2-7B) in two ways: a conventional tactic generator trained only on successful proof paths and TrialMaster trained on proofs augmented with failed branches and backtracking history. At inference time, TrialMaster conditions on the full search history and can emit either Lean tactics or explicit backtrack instructions, while the baseline uses DFS over sampled tactics. Experiments on in-distribution and harder out-of-distribution theorem splits suggest that training with trial-and-error improves proof success and reduces Lean calls relative to strong DFS configurations, and an ablation comparing identical inference style with/without trial-and-error training shows a sizable gain.
strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful train-test mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful traces but used within search procedures that encounter many failures.
The proposed dataset contribution is potentially valuable: Lean formalization plus proof traces with backtracking information could support controlled study of search-aware theorem proving.
The experimental question is clear and the main empirical finding—that trial-and-error supervision can improve theorem proving performance—is intuitively important.
The ablation comparing a model trained with versus without trial-and-error under similar inference style is a useful attempt to isolate the contribution of failure-aware training.
Using Lean for tactic checking ensures proof correctness of accepted outputs and makes evaluation objective.
The paper reports both success rate and search cost (Lean calls), which is appropriate for theorem proving systems where efficiency matters.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is confined to intuitionistic propositional logic, a highly restricted domain, so claims about broader theorem proving utility are limited.

The comparison between TrialMaster and the DFS baseline is not fully apples-to-apples because the systems differ simultaneously in training data, inference procedure, search strategy, and failure criteria.

Several presentation inconsistencies reduce trustworthiness, including duplicated/conflicting Table 3 values (69.3% vs 88.7% for TrialMaster on OOD) and unclear references to shortest four versus shortest five proofs.

The paper claims the dataset is 'uniformly sampled from all possible theorems' and 'representative,' but the actual sampling is conditioned on fixed internal-node count and bounded atoms, which weakens the stated representativeness.

The method relies on a handcrafted proof generator/search procedure whose biases may strongly shape both training and evaluation, raising concerns that the model is learning the generator’s style rather than general proof search principles.
The baseline space is narrow: no comparison to BFS, best-first search, value-guided search, or prior failure-aware prompting/repair methods adapted to this setting.
Statistical rigor is limited: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple training runs despite relatively modest test sets of 1000 theorems each.
The paper does not analyze failure modes in depth, e.g., whether gains come from avoiding repeated tactics, better tactic ranking, or simply learning the proof generator’s backtracking syntax.
methodological_flaws: The central baseline comparison is confounded. TrialMaster is compared against a DFS system that differs not only in training supervision but also in decoding (greedy single-step with explicit backtrack tokens vs multi-sample stochastic DFS), stopping rules, and use of backtracking. This makes it difficult to attribute gains specifically to learning from failed paths.

The evaluation protocol is asymmetric: TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, whereas DFS can continue exploring alternative sampled tactics at a state. Conversely, TrialMaster's backtrack instructions incur no Lean calls, making the search-cost metric favorable by construction. These design differences complicate claims of superior efficiency.

The paper explicitly introduces an incomplete proof-generation/search assumption ('once an implication is picked, the implication cannot be used to show its premise'). Since training and evaluation data are generated under this restriction, the learned task may not faithfully represent full intuitionistic propositional proving, and completeness claims about the dataset/search are overstated.

The claim of 'uniformly sampling from all possible theorems' is scientifically imprecise. A bijection from naturals to formulas does not by itself induce a meaningful uniform distribution over an infinite set; in practice the experiments fix theorem size (16 internal nodes) and bounded atoms, so the sampling is only within a restricted finite slice.

There are internal inconsistencies in reported results. Table 3 appears twice with conflicting TrialMaster success rates (69.3% and 88.7%) while both are described as OOD ablations. Such contradictions undermine empirical validity and make it unclear which numbers support the conclusions.

The train/test split based on proof-length quantiles from proofs generated by the same deterministic/randomized FPS procedure may not establish genuine distribution shift; it may mainly separate easier and harder instances according to the generator’s own notion of proof length.

The exploratory study on proof length changes multiple factors in data selection and does not control for token budget or theorem difficulty, so the conclusion that longer trial-and-error traces reduce quality is not well supported.

No evidence is provided that the model's emitted backtrack instructions are semantically correct beyond formatting and pointing to existing states; thus the claim that the model has learned backtracking capability is only partially validated.
